report:
**Conclusion:** *Possibly, but the evidence does not justify a firm “yes” for routine care.* In type 2 diabetes, pooled randomized-trial evidence suggests probiotics can produce **small average improvements** in blood-sugar measures, especially HbA1c and sometimes fasting glucose/insulin resistance. For example, a 2024 meta-analysis estimated an HbA1c reduction of **0.33 percentage points** (95% CI −0.59 to −0.07)—a modest effect that is much smaller and less established than standard glucose-lowering treatment.  
https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11303337/

The important limitation is consistency: trials use different bacterial strains, doses, food vs. supplement formulations, treatment lengths (often only weeks), baseline glucose levels, and concurrent medications. Meta-analyses report heterogeneity, and individual trials can be null; a recent randomized controlled trial notes that a prior nine-trial review found no significant fasting-glucose effect after 12 weeks.  
https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/endocrinology/articles/10.3389/fendo.2024.1440286/full  
https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38022046/

Clinical guidance therefore remains cautious: Endotext states there is insufficient evidence to recommend probiotics for glycemic control in people with diabetes. They should not replace prescribed medication, nutrition changes, physical activity, or glucose monitoring.  
https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK279012/

If considering one, discuss the specific product with your diabetes clinician—especially if immunocompromised or seriously ill, as long-term safety data are limited and serious infections have been reported in vulnerable groups.  
https://www.nccih.nih.gov/health/probiotics-usefulness-and-safety
